Moment Explosions in the Rough Heston ModelThanks: Financial support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) under grants P 24880 and P 30750 is gratefully acknowledged. We thank Omar El Euch, Antoine Jacquier, and Martin Keller-Ressel for helpful comments.

Stefan Gerhold, Christoph Gerstenecker, Arpad Pinter Email address: sgerhold@fam.tuwien.ac.at Address: FAM, TU Wien
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We show that the moment explosion time in the rough Heston model [El Euch, Rosenbaum 2016, arxiv:1609.02108] is finite if and only if it is finite for the classical Heston model. Upper and lower bounds for the explosion time are established, as well as an algorithm to compute the explosion time (under some restrictions). We show that the critical moments are finite for all maturities. For negative correlation, we apply our algorithm for the moment explosion time to compute the lower critical moment.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
91G20,45D05

1. Introduction

It has long been known that the marginal distributions of a realistic asset price model should not feature tails that are too thin (as, e.g., in the Black-Scholes model). In many models that have been proposed, the tails are of power law type. Consequently, not all moments of the asset price are finite. Existence of the moments has been thoroughly investigated for classical models; in particular, we mention here Keller-Ressel’s work [20] on affine stochastic volatility models. Precise information on the critical moments – the exponents where the stock price ceases to be integrable, depending on maturity – is of interest for several reasons. It allows to approximate the wing behavior of the volatility smile, to assess the convergence rate of some numerical procedures, and to identify models that would assign infinite prices to certain financial products. We refer to [3, 20] and the article Moment Explosions in [8] for further details and references on these motivations. Moreover, when using the Fourier representation to price options, choosing a good integration path (equivalently, a good damping parameter) to avoid highly oscillatory integrands requires knowing the strip of analyticity of the characteristic function. Its boundaries are described by the critical moments [24, 26].

In recent years, attention has shifted in financial modeling from the classical (jump-)diffusion and Lévy models to rough volatility models. Since the pioneering work by Gatheral et al. [15], the literature on these non-Markovian stochastic volatility models, inspired by fractional Brownian motion, has grown rapidly. We refer, e.g., to Bayer et al. [4] for many references. In the present paper we provide some results on the explosion time and the critical moments of the rough Heston model. While there are several “rough” variants of the Heston model, we work with the one proposed by El Euch and Rosenbaum [9]. The dynamics of this model are given by

d​St\displaystyle dS_{t} =St​Vt​d​Wt,S0>0,\displaystyle=S_{t}\sqrt{V_{t}}\,dW_{t},\quad S_{0}>0,
Vt\displaystyle V_{t} =V0+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​(v¯−Vs)​𝑑s+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​ξ​Vs​d​Zs,\displaystyle=V_{0}+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda(\bar{v}-V_{s})\,ds+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\xi\sqrt{V_{s}}\,dZ_{s},
d​⟨W,Z⟩t\displaystyle d\langle W,Z\rangle_{t} =ρ​d​t,\displaystyle=\rho\,dt,

where WW and ZZ are correlated Brownian motions, ρ∈(−1,1)\rho\in(-1,1), and λ,\lambda, ξ,\xi, v¯\bar{v} are positive parameters. The smoothness parameter α\alpha is in (12,1)(\tfrac{1}{2},1). (For α=1\alpha=1, the model clearly reduces to the classical Heston model.) Besides having a microstructural foundation, this model features a characteristic function that can be evaluated numerically in an efficient way, by solving a fractional Riccati equation (equivalently, a non-linear Volterra integral equation; see Section 2). Its tractability makes the rough Heston model attractive for practical implementation, and at the same time facilitates our analysis.

We first analyze the explosion time, i.e., the maturity at which a fixed moment explodes. While the explosion time of the classical Heston model has an explicit formula, for rough Heston we arrive at a well-known hard problem: Computing the explosion time of the solution of a non-linear Volterra integral equation (VIE) of the second kind. There is no general algorithm known, and in most cases that have been studied in the literature, only bounds are available. See Roberts [30] for an overview. Using the specific structure of our case, we show that the explosion time is finite if and only if it is finite for the classical Heston model, and we provide a lower and an upper bound (Sections 3–5). As a byproduct, the validity of the fractional Riccati equation, respectively the VIE, for all moments is established, which culminates in Section 6. In Section 7 we derive an algorithm to compute the explosion time, under some restrictions on the parameters. The critical moments are finite for all maturities (Section 8) and can be computed by numerical root finding (Section 9). Our approach has two limitations: First, to compute the critical moments, maturity must not be too high. Second, our algorithm can compute the upper critical moment only for ρ>0\rho>0, and the lower critical moment for ρ<0\rho<0. As the latter is the more important case in practice, we focus on the left wing of implied volatility when recalling the relation between critical moments and strike asymptotics (Lee’s moment formula; see Section 10).

Corollary 3.1 in [10] is related to our results. For each maturity, it gives explicit lower and upper bounds for the critical moments. Inverting them yields a lower bound for the explosion time; the latter is not comparable to our bounds.

2. Preliminaries

El Euch and Rosenbaum [9] established a semi-explicit representation of the moment generating function (mgf) of the log-price Xt=log⁡(St/S0)X_{t}=\log(S_{t}/S_{0}) in the rough Heston model. The mgf is given by

(2.1) 𝔼⁡[eu​Xt]=exp⁡(v¯​λ​It1​ψ​(u,t)+v0​It1−α​ψ​(u,t)),\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{t}}]=\exp\big(\bar{v}\lambda I^{1}_{t}\psi(u,t)+v_{0}I^{1-\alpha}_{t}\psi(u,t)\big),

where ψ\psi satisfies a fractional Riccati differential equation (see below). The constraint ρ∈(−1/2,1/2]\rho\in(-1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2}] from [9] was removed recently in [10]. The paper [2] contains an alternative derivation of the fractional Riccati equation, and [1] has more general results, embedding the rough Heston model into the new class of affine Volterra processes. Recall the following definition (see e.g. [21]):

Definition 2.1.

The (left-sided) Riemann-Liouville fractional integral ItαI_{t}^{\alpha} of order α∈(0,∞)\alpha\in(0,\infty) of a function ff is given by

(2.2) Itα​f​(t):=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​f​(s)​𝑑sI^{\alpha}_{t}f(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}f(s)\,ds

whenever the integral exists, and the (left-sided) Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative DtαD_{t}^{\alpha} of order α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) of ff is given by

(2.3) Dtα​f​(t):=dd​t​I1−α​f​(t)D^{\alpha}_{t}f(t):=\frac{d}{dt}I^{1-\alpha}f(t)

whenever this expression exists.

(The fractional derivative DtαD^{\alpha}_{t} can be defined for α>1\alpha>1 as well, but this is not needed in our context.) The function ψ\psi from (2.1) is the unique continuous solution of the fractional Riccati initial value problem

(2.5) It1−α​ψ​(u,0)\displaystyle I^{1-\alpha}_{t}\psi(u,0) =0,\displaystyle=0,

Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), T>0T>0 and suppose that ψ∈C⁡[0,T]\psi\in C[0,T] and H∈C⁡(ℝ)H\in C(\mathbb{R}). Then ψ\psi satisfies the fractional differential equation

Theorem 2.3.

Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), g∈C[0,∞)g\in C[0,\infty), and suppose that H:ℝ→ℝH:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is locally Lipschitz continuous. Then there is T∗∈(0,∞]T^{*}\in(0,\infty] such that the Volterra integral equation

  1. (A)

    c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0, e0​(u)≥0,e_{0}(u)\geq 0,

  2. (B)

    c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0, e0​(u)<0e_{0}(u)<0 and e1​(u)<0,e_{1}(u)<0,

  3. (C)

As several of our results deal with ρ<0\rho<0 and uu satisfying case (A), we explicitly note

case (A) for ρ<0:u≤λρ​ξ.\text{case (A) for $\rho<0$:}\qquad u\leq\frac{\lambda}{\rho\xi}.

Note that cases (A) and (B) combined are exactly the cases in which the moment explosion time T1∗​(u)T^{\ast}_{1}(u) in the classical Heston model is finite, by (2.13). We can now state our first main result.

Theorem 2.4.

For u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, the moment explosion time Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{\ast}(u) of the rough Heston model is finite if and only if uu satisfies (A) or (B). This is equivalent to T1∗​(u)T_{1}^{\ast}(u) (explosion time of the classical Heston model) being finite.

The proof of Theorem 2.4 consists of two main parts. First, Propositions 3.2, 3.4, 3.6, and 3.7 discuss the blow-up behavior of the solution of (2.9) in cases (A)-(D), and Lemma 3.8 shows that blow-up of ff leads (unsurprisingly) to blow-up of the right-hand side of (2.1). Second, we show in Section 5 that the explosion time of f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) (the solution of (2.9)) agrees with Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) (the explosion time of the rough Heston model) for all u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}. As mentioned after Theorem 2.3, this is not obvious from the results in the existing literature.

3. Explosion time of the Volterra integral equation

We begin by citing a result from Brunner and Yang [7] which characterizes the blow-up behavior of non-linear Volterra integral equations defined by positive and increasing functions. We note that some arguments in our subsequent proofs (from Proposition 3.2 onwards) are similar to arguments used in [7]. Alternatively, it should be possible to extend the arguments in Appendix A of [16]; there, uu is in [0,1][0,1].

Proposition 3.1.

Assume that G:[0,∞)→[0,∞)G\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) is continuous and the following conditions hold:

  • (G1)

    G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0 and GG is strictly increasing,

  • (G2)

    limw→∞G⁡(w)/w=∞\lim_{w\to\infty}G(w)/w=\infty,

  • (P)

    ϕ:[0,∞)→(0,∞)\phi\colon[0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) is a positive, non-decreasing, continuous function,

  • (K)

    k:(0,∞)→[0,∞)k\colon(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) is locally integrable and K⁡(t):=∫0tk⁡(z)​𝑑z>0K(t):=\int_{0}^{t}k(z)\,dz>0 is a non-decreasing function.

Furthermore, assume limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t)=\infty and k⁡(z)=c​zα−1k(z)=cz^{\alpha-1} with α>0\alpha>0 and c>0c>0. Then the solution hh of the Volterra integral equation

h⁡(t)=ϕ⁡(t)+∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G​(h⁡(s))​𝑑sh(t)=\phi(t)+\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)G(h(s))\,ds

blows up in finite time if and only if

(3.1) ∫U∞(wG⁡(w))1/α​d​ww<∞\int_{U}^{\infty}\left(\frac{w}{G(w)}\right)^{1/\alpha}\frac{dw}{w}<\infty

for all U>0U>0.

Proof.

This is a special case of Corollary 2.22 in Brunner and Yang [7], with GG not depending on time. ∎

In case (A), all assumptions of Proposition 3.1 are satisfied and only the integrability condition (3.1) has to be checked to determine whether the solution ff of (2.9) blows up in finite time.

Proposition 3.2.

In case (A), the solution ff of (2.9) starts at 00, is positive thereafter and blows up in finite time.

Proof.

Fix u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} such that c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0 and e0​(u)≥0e_{0}(u)\geq 0. Note that e02−e1>0e_{0}^{2}-e_{1}>0 in this case. (Here and in the following, we will often suppress uu in the notation.) If we write the Volterra integral equation (2.9) in the form

f⁡(t)=ϕ⁡(t)+∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G¯​(f⁡(s))​𝑑sf(t)=\phi(t)+\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)\bar{G}(f(s))\,ds

with non-linearity G¯​(w)=w2+2​e0​w\bar{G}(w)=w^{2}+2e_{0}w and ϕ⁡(t)=e02−e1Γ⁡(1+α)​tα\phi(t)=\frac{e_{0}^{2}-e_{1}}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}t^{\alpha}, using (2.10) and (7.3), then the conditions c1>0c_{1}>0 and e0≥0e_{0}\geq 0 guarantee that ϕ\phi and G¯\bar{G} are positive and strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) with ϕ​(0)=G¯​(0)=0\phi(0)=\bar{G}(0)=0. Hence, the solution ff is positive for positive values, and f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. (Positivity follows from Lemma 2.4 in [7], or from Lemma 3.2.11 in [6].) It is easy to check that all the assumptions (G1), (G2), (P) and (K) of Proposition 3.1 are satisfied. Moreover, limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t)=\infty and

∫U∞(wG¯​(w))1/α​d​ww≤∫U∞w−1−1/α​𝑑w<∞\displaystyle\int^{\infty}_{U}\left(\frac{w}{\bar{G}(w)}\right)^{1/\alpha}\frac{dw}{w}\leq\int^{\infty}_{U}w^{-1-1/\alpha}\,dw<\infty

for all U>0U>0. By Proposition 3.1, the solution ff blows up in finite time. ∎

In case (B), Proposition 3.1 cannot be applied directly to the solution ff of (2.9). Hence, the Volterra integral equation has to be modified in order to satisfy the assumptions of Proposition 3.1 in a way that ff is still a subsolution of the modified equation, i.e. ff satisfies (2.9) with “≥\geq” instead of “==”. First, we provide a comparison lemma for solutions and subsolutions.

Lemma 3.3.

Let G:[0,∞)→(0,∞)G\colon[0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) be a strictly increasing, continuous function and T>0T>0. Suppose that gg is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra integral equation

f⁡(t)≥∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s,t∈[0,T],f(t)\geq\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)G(f(s))\,ds,\quad t\in[0,T],

For any c∈(0,T)c\in(0,T) define fc​(t):=f⁡(t+c)f_{c}(t):=f(t+c) for t∈[0,T−c]t\in[0,T-c]. From the positivity of GG, it follows that fc​(0)=f⁡(c)>0f_{c}(0)=f(c)>0 and

0=fc​(t)−g⁡(t)≥∫0tk⁡(t−s)​(G⁡(fc​(s))−G⁡(g⁡(s)))​𝑑s>0,0=f_{c}(t)-g(t)\geq\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)\big(G(f_{c}(s))-G(g(s))\big)\,ds>0,

Proposition 3.4.

In case (B), the solution ff of (2.9) starts at 00, is positive thereafter and blows up in finite time.

Proof.

Fix u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} such that c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0, e0​(u)<0e_{0}(u)<0 and e1​(u)<0e_{1}(u)<0. Note that in this case, the non-linearity GG is obviously positive by (2.10). However, GG is strictly decreasing on [0,−e1][0,-e_{1}]. To deal with this problem, let 0<a<−e10<a<-e_{1} and define the modified non-linearity G¯a\bar{G}_{a} as

(3.2) G¯a​(w)={w​a+e1e0+a,0≤w<−e0,G⁡(w),w≥−e0.\bar{G}_{a}(w)=\begin{cases}w\frac{a+e_{1}}{e_{0}}+a,&0\leq w<-e_{0},\\ G(w),&w\geq-e_{0}.\end{cases}

Then G¯a\bar{G}_{a} is a positive, strictly increasing, Lipschitz continuous function that starts at aa and G¯a≤G\bar{G}_{a}\leq G. Let f¯\bar{f} be the unique continuous solution (recall Theorem 2.3) of the Volterra integral equation

(3.3) f¯​(t)=∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G¯a​(f¯​(s))​𝑑s=ϕ⁡(t)+∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G¯​(f¯​(s))​𝑑s\bar{f}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)\bar{G}_{a}(\bar{f}(s))\,ds=\phi(t)+\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)\bar{G}(\bar{f}(s))\,ds

with G¯=G¯a−a\bar{G}=\bar{G}_{a}-a and ϕ⁡(t)=aΓ⁡(1+α)​tα\phi(t)=\frac{a}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}t^{\alpha}. Note that the second equality in (3.3) follows from (7.3). Due to the positivity of ϕ\phi and G¯\bar{G} on (0,∞)(0,\infty), the solution f¯\bar{f} is positive on (0,∞)(0,\infty) as well. The functions ϕ\phi, G¯\bar{G} and kk satisfy the assumptions (G1), (G2), (P) and (K) in Proposition 3.1. Furthermore, limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t)=\infty and G¯\bar{G} satisfies (3.1). By Proposition 3.1, f¯\bar{f} blows up in finite time. Because ff satisfies (2.9) and G¯a≤G\bar{G}_{a}\leq G, it follows that ff is a subsolution of the modified Volterra integral equation, i.e.,

f⁡(t)≥∫0tk⁡(t−s)​G¯a​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s.f(t)\geq\int_{0}^{t}k(t-s)\bar{G}_{a}(f(s))\,ds.

Now, Lemma 3.3 implies f≥f¯f\geq\bar{f}. Consequently, ff blows up as well. ∎

Cases (C) and (D) are the cases where the solution ff of (2.9) does not blow up in finite time. In fact, ff does not blow up at all, as we will see. The following lemma provides the key argument for both cases.

Lemma 3.5.

Let G:[0,∞)→[0,∞)G\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) be a Lipschitz continuous function that is positive on [0,a)[0,a) and G≡0G\equiv 0 on [a,∞)[a,\infty) for an a>0a>0. Then the unique continuous solution ff of the Volterra integral equation

Proof.

The non-negativity of GG implies f≥0f\geq 0. Suppose t>0t>0 exists such that f⁡(t)>af(t)>a. By the continuity of ff, there exists 0<t0<t0<t_{0}<t that satisfies f⁡(t0)=af(t_{0})=a and f⁡(s)>af(s)>a for all s∈(t0,t)s\in(t_{0},t). From G≡0G\equiv 0 on [a,∞)[a,\infty), we have

∫t0tk⁡(t−s)​G​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s=0.\int_{t_{0}}^{t}k(t-s)G(f(s))\,ds=0.

Since GG is non-negative and kk is decreasing,

0\displaystyle 0 <f⁡(t)−f⁡(t0)\displaystyle<f(t)-f(t_{0})
=∫t0tk⁡(t−s)​G​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s+∫0t0(k⁡(t−s)−k⁡(t0−s))​G​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s\displaystyle=\int_{t_{0}}^{t}k(t-s)G(f(s))\,ds+\int_{0}^{t_{0}}\big(k(t-s)-k(t_{0}-s)\big)G(f(s))\,ds
=∫0t0(k⁡(t−s)−k⁡(t0−s))​G​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s≤0,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t_{0}}\big(k(t-s)-k(t_{0}-s)\big)G(f(s))\,ds\leq 0,

which is a contradiction. Therefore, ff satisfies 0≤f⁡(t)≤a0\leq f(t)\leq a for all t≥0t\geq 0. ∎

Proposition 3.6.

In case (C), the solution ff of (2.9) is non-negative and bounded, and exists globally.

Proof.

Fix u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} such that c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0, e0​(u)<0e_{0}(u)<0 and e1​(u)≥0e_{1}(u)\geq 0. and from the uniqueness of the solution we obtain f=f¯f=\bar{f}. ∎

We have shown that (A) and (B) are exactly the cases in which the solution ff of the Volterra integral equation (2.9), and thus the solution ψ\psi of the fractional Riccati differential equation (2.4) with initial value (2.5), blows up in finite time. The following lemma shows that blow-up of ψ\psi is equivalent to blow-up of the right-hand side of (2.1).

Lemma 3.8.

If ff is a non-negative, continuous function that blows up in finite time with explosion time T^\hat{T}, then Itα​fI^{\alpha}_{t}f blows up in finite time as well, with the same explosion time T^\hat{T}. If ff is a bounded continuous function, then Itα​fI^{\alpha}_{t}f does not blow up in finite time.

Proof.

First, suppose that the non-negative, continuous function ff explodes at T^\hat{T} and let M>0M>0. Then we can find ε∈(0,T^/2)\varepsilon\in(0,\hat{T}/2) such that f⁡(t)≥Mf(t)\geq M for all t∈(T^−ε,T^)t\in(\hat{T}-\varepsilon,\hat{T}). Hence,

Itα​f​(t)\displaystyle I^{\alpha}_{t}f(t) ≥∫T∗−εtk⁡(t−s)​f​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\geq\int_{T^{\ast}-\varepsilon}^{t}k(t-s)f(s)\,ds
≥M​(T^−ε)αΓ⁡(1+α)≥M​(T^/2)αΓ⁡(1+α)\displaystyle\geq M\frac{(\hat{T}-\varepsilon)^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}\geq M\frac{(\hat{T}/2)^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}

for all t∈(T^−ε,T^)t\in(\hat{T}-\varepsilon,\hat{T}). For the second assertion, suppose that ff is continuous and bounded with M>0M>0. Then we have

|Itα​f​(t)|≤MΓ⁡(1+α)​tα|I^{\alpha}_{t}f(t)|\leq\frac{M}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}t^{\alpha}

for all t≥0t\geq 0. ∎

4. Bounds for the explosion time

We now establish lower and upper bounds for T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u), valid whenever it is finite (cases (A) and (B)). We denote by T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) the explosion time of the solution f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) of (2.9). As we will see later, it agrees with Tα∗​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u), and so both bounds of this section hold for the explosion time of the rough Heston model. We prove them first, because we will apply the lower bound in the proof of Tα∗​(u)=T^α​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u)=\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u).

Theorem 4.1.

In cases (A) and (B), the blow-up time T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) of the solution f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) of (2.9) satisfies

(4.1) T^α​(u)≥Γ​(1+α)1/α​maxr>1​(rα−1)1/αr⁡(r−1)​∫a⁡(u)∞(wG⁡(u,w))1/α​d​ww,\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\geq\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\max_{r>1}\frac{(r^{\alpha}-1)^{1/\alpha}}{r(r-1)}\int_{a(u)}^{\infty}\bigg(\frac{w}{G(u,w)}\bigg)^{1/\alpha}\frac{dw}{w},

where a⁡(u)=0a(u)=0 in case (A) and a⁡(u)=−e0​(u)>0a(u)=-e_{0}(u)>0 in case (B).

Proof.

Fix uu satisfying the requirements of case (A) or (B). It follows from Propositions 3.2 and 3.4 that in either case the solution ff is non-negative, starts at 00 and limt↑T^αf⁡(t)=∞\lim_{t\uparrow\hat{T}_{\alpha}}f(t)=\infty. For any n∈N0n\in\mathrm{N}_{0} choose

tn:=min⁡{t>0:f⁡(t)=(c​rn)α+a}t_{n}:=\min\{t>0:f(t)=(cr^{n})^{\alpha}+a\}

with r>1r>1 and c>0c>0. Using the inequality k⁡(tn−s)<k⁡(tn−1−s)k(t_{n}-s)<k(t_{n-1}-s) for s∈(0,tn−1)s\in(0,t_{n-1}), the non-negativity of GG and that GG is strictly increasing on [a,∞)[a,\infty), we have for n∈Nn\in\mathrm{N}

≤f⁡(tn−1)+G⁡(f⁡(tn))​∫tn−1tnk⁡(tn−s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq f(t_{n-1})+G(f(t_{n}))\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_{n}}k(t_{n}-s)\,ds
=f⁡(tn−1)+1Γ⁡(1+α)​G​(f⁡(tn))​(tn−tn−1)α.\displaystyle=f(t_{n-1})+\frac{1}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}G(f(t_{n}))(t_{n}-t_{n-1})^{\alpha}.

Thus, we obtain for n∈Nn\in\mathrm{N}

tn−tn−1\displaystyle t_{n}-t_{n-1} ≥Γ​(1+α)1/α​(f⁡(tn)−f⁡(tn−1)G⁡(f⁡(tn)))1/α\displaystyle\geq\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\left(\frac{f(t_{n})-f(t_{n-1})}{G(f(t_{n}))}\right)^{1/\alpha}
=Γ​(1+α)1/α​(rα−1)1/α​c​rn−1G​((c​rn)α+a)1/α\displaystyle=\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}(r^{\alpha}-1)^{1/\alpha}\frac{cr^{n-1}}{G((cr^{n})^{\alpha}+a)^{1/\alpha}}
=Γ​(1+α)1/α​(rα−1)1/αr⁡(r−1)⋅c​rn+1−c​rnG​((c​rn)α+a)1/α\displaystyle=\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{(r^{\alpha}-1)^{1/\alpha}}{r(r-1)}\cdot\frac{cr^{n+1}-cr^{n}}{G((cr^{n})^{\alpha}+a)^{1/\alpha}}
≥Γ​(1+α)1/α​(rα−1)1/αr⁡(r−1)​∫c​rnc​rn+1(1G⁡(sα+a))1/α​𝑑s.\displaystyle\geq\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{(r^{\alpha}-1)^{1/\alpha}}{r(r-1)}\int_{cr^{n}}^{cr^{n+1}}\left(\frac{1}{G(s^{\alpha}+a)}\right)^{1/\alpha}\,ds.

Finally,

T^α\displaystyle\hat{T}_{\alpha} =t0+∑n=1∞(tn−tn−1)\displaystyle=t_{0}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(t_{n}-t_{n-1})
≥Γ​(1+α)1/α​(rα−1)1/αr⁡(r−1)​∫c​r∞(1G⁡(sα+a))1/α​𝑑s.\displaystyle\geq\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{(r^{\alpha}-1)^{1/\alpha}}{r(r-1)}\int_{cr}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{G(s^{\alpha}+a)}\right)^{1/\alpha}\,ds.

For α↑1\alpha\uparrow 1, the right-hand side of (4.1) simplifies to

In case (A), the lower bound (4.1) is sharp in the limit α↑1\alpha\uparrow 1: We have a⁡(u)=0a(u)=0 then, and therefore (4.2) is exactly the moment explosion time (2.12) of the classical Heston model.

Another lower bound for T^α\hat{T}_{\alpha} can be obtained from Corollary 3.1 in [10]. Numerical examples show that it is not comparable to the bound from our Theorem 4.1.

Theorem 4.2.

In cases (A) and (B), the blow-up time T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) of the solution f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) of (2.9) satisfies

(4.3) T^α​(u)≤4​Γ​(1+α)1/α​∫0∞(wG^​(u,w))1/α​d​ww,\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\leq 4\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigg(\frac{w}{\hat{G}(u,w)}\bigg)^{1/\alpha}\frac{dw}{w},

where G^=G\hat{G}=G in case (A), and G^≡−e1\hat{G}\equiv-e_{1} on [0,−e0)[0,-e_{0}) and G^=G\hat{G}=G on [−e0,∞)[-e_{0},\infty) in case (B).

Proof.

Fix uu satisfying the requirements of case (A) or (B). From Propositions 3.2 and 3.4, in either case the solution ff is positive on (0,∞)(0,\infty), starts at 00 and limt↑T^αf⁡(t)=∞\lim_{t\uparrow\hat{T}_{\alpha}}f(t)=\infty. For any n∈N0n\in\mathrm{N}_{0} choose

(4.4) tn:=max⁡{t<T^α:f⁡(t)=(c​rn)α}t_{n}:=\max\{t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}:f(t)=(cr^{n})^{\alpha}\}

with r>1r>1 and c>0c>0. Define G¯:=G\bar{G}:=G in case (A) and G¯:=G¯a\bar{G}:=\bar{G}_{a} from (3.2) in case (B). Since G¯≤G\bar{G}\leq G and G¯\bar{G} is positive and strictly increasing, we have for n∈Nn\in\mathrm{N}

f⁡(tn)\displaystyle f(t_{n}) ≥∫0tnk⁡(tn−s)​G¯​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s\displaystyle\geq\int_{0}^{t_{n}}k(t_{n}-s)\bar{G}(f(s))\,ds
≥∫tn−1tnk⁡(tn−s)​G¯​(f⁡(s))​𝑑s\displaystyle\geq\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_{n}}k(t_{n}-s)\bar{G}(f(s))\,ds
≥1Γ⁡(1+α)​G¯​(f⁡(tn−1))​(tn−tn−1)α.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\Gamma(1+\alpha)}\bar{G}(f(t_{n-1}))(t_{n}-t_{n-1})^{\alpha}.

tn−tn−1\displaystyle t_{n}-t_{n-1} ≤Γ​(1+α)1/α​(f⁡(tn)G¯​(f​(tn−1)))1/α\displaystyle\leq\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\left(\frac{f(t_{n})}{\bar{G}(f(t_{n-1}))}\right)^{1/\alpha}
=Γ​(1+α)1/α​c​rnG¯​((c​rn−1)α)1/α\displaystyle=\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{cr^{n}}{\bar{G}((cr^{n-1})^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}}
=Γ​(1+α)1/α​r2r−1⋅c​rn−1−c​rn−2G¯​((c​rn−1)α)1/α\displaystyle=\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{r^{2}}{r-1}\cdot\frac{cr^{n-1}-cr^{n-2}}{\bar{G}((cr^{n-1})^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}}

Therefore,

≤t0+Γ​(1+α)1/α​r2r−1​∫c​r−1∞(1G¯​(sα))1/α​𝑑s.\displaystyle\leq t_{0}+\Gamma(1+\alpha)^{1/\alpha}\frac{r^{2}}{r-1}\int_{cr^{-1}}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{G}(s^{\alpha})}\right)^{1/\alpha}\,ds.

See Figures 1–3 for numerical examples of these bounds.

5. Explosion time in the rough Heston model

In Section 3, we established that the right-hand side of (2.1), defined using the solution ff of the VIE (2.9), explodes if and only if uu satisfies the conditions of cases (A) or (B). As before, we write T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) for the explosion time of f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot). Recall that Tα∗​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u) denotes the explosion time of the rough Heston model, as defined in (2.11). The goal of the present section is to show that T^α​(u)=Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)=T^{*}_{\alpha}(u), and that (2.1) holds for all u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} and 0<t<Tα∗​(u)0<t<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u). The following result from [10] was already mentioned at the end of the introduction.

Lemma 5.1 (Corollary 3.1 in [10]).

For each t>0t>0, there is an open interval such that (2.1) holds for all uu from that interval.

Lemma 5.2.

The solution ff of the Volterra integral equation (2.9) is differentiable w.r.t. uu, and its derivative satisfies

(5.1) ∂1f⁡(u,t)=∫0t(t−s)α−1Γ⁡(α)​(∂1G⁡(u,f⁡(u,s))+∂2G⁡(u,f⁡(u,s))​∂1f⁡(u,s))​𝑑s.\displaystyle\partial_{1}f(u,t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{(t-s)^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\Big(\partial_{1}G(u,f(u,s))+\partial_{2}G(u,f(u,s))\partial_{1}f(u,s)\Big)ds.
Proof.

We check the requirements of Theorem 13.1.2 in Gripenberg et al. [19]. The polynomial G⁡(u,w)G(u,w) is differentiable. The kernel (t−s)α−1/Γ⁡(α)=:k⁡(t−s)(t-s)^{\alpha-1}/\Gamma(\alpha)=:k(t-s) is of continuous type in the sense of [19]; see the remark to Theorem 12.1.1 there, which states local integrability of kk as a sufficient condition for this property. ∎

Lemma 5.3.
  • (i)

    In case (A) we have ∂1f⁡(u,t)<0\partial_{1}f(u,t)<0 for u<0u<0 and ∂1f⁡(u,t)>0\partial_{1}f(u,t)>0 for u>0u>0.

  • (ii)

    If uu satisfies case (B), then the same holds if T^α​(u)−t\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)-t is sufficiently small.

Proof.

We only discuss the case u<0u<0, because u>0u>0 is analogous.

(i) Note that (5.1) is a “linear VIE” that can be written as

(5.2) ∂1f⁡(u,t)=g⁡(t)+∫0t(t−s)α−1​K(u)​(t,s)​∂1f⁡(u,s)​𝑑s,\partial_{1}f(u,t)=g(t)+\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}K^{(u)}(t,s)\partial_{1}f(u,s)\,ds,

where we define

(5.3) g⁡(t)\displaystyle g(t) :=∫0t(t−s)α−1Γ⁡(α)​∂1G⁡(u,f⁡(u,s))​𝑑s,\displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{(t-s)^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\partial_{1}G(u,f(u,s))\,ds,
(5.4) K(u)​(t,s)\displaystyle K^{(u)}(t,s) =K(u)​(s):=∂2G⁡(u,f⁡(u,s))Γ⁡(α)\displaystyle=K^{(u)}(s):=\frac{\partial_{2}G(u,f(u,s))}{\Gamma(\alpha)}

to bring the notation close to that of Section 6.1.2 in [5]. Clearly, (5.2) is not really a linear VIE, because the unknown function ff appears in gg and K(u)K^{(u)}. But as our aim is not to solve it, but to control the sign of ∂1f\partial_{1}f, this viewpoint is good enough.

As we are in case (A), we get from c1​(u)>0c_{1}(u)>0 and e0​(u)≥0e_{0}(u)\geq 0 that u≤λ/(ρ​ξ)<0u\leq\lambda/(\rho\xi)<0. Furthermore, we have e0′​(u)=ξ​ρ/2<0e_{0}^{\prime}(u)=\xi\rho/2<0, c1′​(u)=u−1/2<0c_{1}^{\prime}(u)=u-1/2<0 and therefore

Lemma 5.4.

Let u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} and 0<t<T^α​(u)0<t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u). Then f⁡(⋅,t)f(\cdot,t) is analytic at uu.

Proof.

According to Section 3.1.1 in [6], the solution can be constructed by successive iteration and continuation. We just show that the first iteration step leads to an analytic function, because the finitely many further steps needed to arrive at arbitrary t<T^α​(u)t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) can be dealt with analogously. Define the iterates f0=0f_{0}=0 and

fn+1​(v,s):=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0s(s−τ)α−1​G​(v,fn​(v,τ))​𝑑τ,n≥0.f_{n+1}(v,s):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{s}(s-\tau)^{\alpha-1}G(v,f_{n}(v,\tau))d\tau,\quad n\geq 0.

On a sufficiently small time interval, fn​(v,⋅)f_{n}(v,\cdot) converges uniformly to f⁡(v,⋅)f(v,\cdot), and the solution can then be continued by solving an updated integral equation and so on (see [6]), until we hit T^α​(v)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(v). Now fix uu and tt as in the statement of the lemma. For a sufficiently small open complex neighborhood U∋uU\ni u, it is easy to see that t<T^α​(v)t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(v) holds for v∈Uv\in U. Define

γ:=1∨supv∈U|v|andη:=1∨tαΓ⁡(α+1).\gamma:=1\vee\sup_{v\in U}|v|\quad\text{and}\quad\eta:=1\vee\frac{t^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}.

Then there is c≥1c\geq 1 such that, for arbitrary v∈Uv\in U and w∈ℂw\in\mathbb{C},

|G⁡(v,w)|\displaystyle|G(v,w)| ≤c⁡((|w|∨1)2∨γ⁡(|w|∨1)∨γ2)\displaystyle\leq c\big((|w|\vee 1)^{2}\vee\gamma(|w|\vee 1)\vee\gamma^{2}\big)
≤c​γ2​(|w|∨1)2=:θ​(|w|∨1)2.\displaystyle\leq c\gamma^{2}(|w|\vee 1)^{2}=:\theta(|w|\vee 1)^{2}.

By the definition of fnf_{n}, a trivial inductive proof then shows that

(5.13) supv∈Us∈[0,t]|fn​(v,s)|≤(θ​η)2n−1,n≥0.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in U\\ s\in[0,t]\end{subarray}}|f_{n}(v,s)|\leq(\theta\eta)^{2^{n}-1},\quad n\geq 0.

By a standard result on parameter integrals (Theorem IV.5.8 in [11]), the bound (5.13) implies that each function fn​(⋅,t)f_{n}(\cdot,t) is analytic in UU. From the bounds in Section 3.1.1 of [6], it is very easy to see that the convergence fn​(v,t)→f⁡(v,t)f_{n}(v,t)\to f(v,t) is locally uniform w.r.t. vv for fixed tt. It is well known (see Theorem 3.5.1 in [18]) that this implies that the limit function f⁡(⋅,t)f(\cdot,t) is analytic. ∎

Lemma 5.5.

The function u↦T^α​(u)u\mapsto\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) increases for u≤0u\leq 0 and decreases for u≥1u\geq 1.

Proof.

Recall that T^α​(u)=∞\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)=\infty in cases (C) and (D), which include u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. For case (A), the assertion follows from part (i) of Lemma 5.3. So let uu satisfy case (B), where again we assume w.l.o.g. that u<0u<0. Suppose that T^α​(⋅)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(\cdot) does not increase. Then we can pick u0<0u_{0}<0 such that any left neighborhood of u0u_{0} contains a point uu with T^α​(u)>T^α​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)>\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0}). From the continuity of ∂1f\partial_{1}f (see Lemma 5.4), part (ii) of Lemma 5.3, and the continuity of τ\tau from (5.8), there are u1<u0u_{1}<u_{0} satisfying T^α​(u1)>T^α​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})>\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0}) and t1<T^α​(u0)t_{1}<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0}) such that ∂1f⁡(u,t)<0\partial_{1}f(u,t)<0 in the rectangle

{(u,t):u1≤u≤u0,t1≤t<T^α(u1)}.\{(u,t):u_{1}\leq u\leq u_{0},t_{1}\leq t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})\}.

Then, limt↑T^α​(u0)f⁡(u0,t)=∞\lim_{t\uparrow\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0})}f(u_{0},t)=\infty implies that

(5.14) limt↑T^α​(u0)f⁡(u1,t)=∞,\lim_{t\uparrow\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0})}f(u_{1},t)=\infty,

because the inequality ∂1f⁡(u,t)<0\partial_{1}f(u,t)<0 shows that f⁡(u1,⋅)f(u_{1},\cdot) must explode at least as fast as f⁡(u0,⋅)f(u_{0},\cdot). But (5.14) is a contradiction to T^α​(u1)>T^α​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})>\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0}). ∎

Lemma 5.6.

Let u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} and 0<t<T^α​(u)0<t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u). Then (2.1) holds, where (as above) f=c3​ψf=c_{3}\psi and f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) is the solution of (2.9).

Proof.

We assume that u<0u<0, as u≥0u\geq 0 is handled analogously. By Lemma 5.5, u↦T^α​(u)u\mapsto\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) increases. In this proof, we write M⁡(u,t)M(u,t) for the right-hand side of (2.1), and M~​(u,t)=𝔼⁡[eu​Xt]\tilde{M}(u,t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{t}}] for the mgf. Now fix u<0u<0 and 0<t<T^α​(u)0<t<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) such that (u,t)(u,t) has positive distance from the graph of the increasing function T^α​(⋅)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(\cdot). Clearly, it suffices to consider pairs (u,t)(u,t) with this property. By Lemma 5.1, there are v−<v+v^{-}<v^{+} such that

(5.15) M⁡(v,t)=M~​(v,t),v−<v<v+.M(v,t)=\tilde{M}(v,t),\quad v^{-}<v<v^{+}.

We now show that (5.15) extends to u≤v≤v+u\leq v\leq v^{+} by analytic continuation. From general results on characteristic functions (Theorems II.5a and II.5b in [34]), v↦M~​(v,t)v\mapsto\tilde{M}(v,t) is analytic in a vertical strip w−<Re⁡(v)<w+w^{-}<\mathrm{Re}(v)<w^{+} of the complex plane, and has a singularity at v=w−v=w^{-}. If we suppose that w−>uw^{-}>u, then Lemma 5.4 leads to a contradiction: The left-hand side of (5.15) would then be analytic at v=w−v=w^{-}, and the right-hand side singular. This shows that (5.15) can be extended to the left up to uu by analytic continuation. ∎

The following theorem completes the proof of Theorem 2.4.

Theorem 5.7.

Let u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}. Then T^α​(u)=Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)=T^{*}_{\alpha}(u), and (2.1) holds for 0<t<Tα∗​(u)0<t<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u).

Proof.

In the light of Lemma 5.6, it only remains to show that T^α​(u)≥Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\geq T^{*}_{\alpha}(u). (Obviously, Lemma 5.6 implies that T^α​(u)≤Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\leq T^{*}_{\alpha}(u).) But this is clear from the continuity of the map t↦M~​(u,t)=𝔼⁡[eu​Xt]t\mapsto\tilde{M}(u,t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{t}}] on the interval (0,Tα∗​(u))(0,T^{*}_{\alpha}(u)). This continuity follows from the continuity of t↦Xtt\mapsto X_{t}, Doob’s submartingale inequality, and dominated convergence. ∎

For later use (Section 9), we give the following alternative argument:

Another proof that T^α​(u)≥Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\geq T^{*}_{\alpha}(u).

Let us suppose that there is u0u_{0} with T^α​(u0)<Tα∗​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0})<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u_{0}). From Theorem 4.1, it is easy to see that the continuous function u↦T^α​(u)u\mapsto\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) tends to +∞+\infty as u<0u<0 approaches the region where T^α​(u)=∞\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)=\infty. Thus, there is u1>u0u_{1}>u_{0} with T^α​(u0)<T^α​(u1)<Tα∗​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{0})<\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u_{0}).

We have seen in Lemma 5.4 that u↦f⁡(u,t)u\mapsto f(u,t) is analytic for any fixed tt. But it is also analytic w.r.t. tt for fixed uu: From Theorem 1 in Lubich [27], itself based on earlier work by Miller and Feldstein [28], it follows that f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) is analytic on the whole interval (0,T^α​(u))(0,\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)). By Hartogs’s theorem (Theorem 1.2.5 in [22]), we conclude that the bivariate function f⁡(⋅,⋅)f(\cdot,\cdot) is continuous. Thus, the blow-up of f⁡(u1,⋅)f(u_{1},\cdot) at T^α​(u1)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1}) implies that

(5.16) limu↓u1M⁡(u,T^α​(u1))=∞.\lim_{u\downarrow u_{1}}M(u,\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1}))=\infty.

(Again, we write MM for the right-hand side of (2.1) and M~\tilde{M} for the mgf.) By Lemma 5.6, M~​(⋅,T^α​(u1))\tilde{M}(\cdot,\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})) also blows up there, and thus has a singularity at u1u_{1}. Since u0<u1u_{0}<u_{1}, we conclude from Corollary II.1b in [34] that M~​(u0,T^α​(u1))=∞\tilde{M}(u_{0},\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1}))=\infty. As S=eXS=e^{X} is a martingale, this implies that M~​(u0,t)=∞\tilde{M}(u_{0},t)=\infty for all t≥T^α​(u1)t\geq\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1}). In particular, it contradicts T^α​(u1)<Tα∗​(u0)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u_{1})<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u_{0}). ∎

6. Validity of the fractional Riccati equation for complex uu

Although the focus of this paper is on real uu, the mgf needs to be evaluated at complex arguments when used for option pricing. The following result fully justifies using the fractional Riccati equation (2.4), respectively the VIE (2.9), to do so. As above, we write Tα∗​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u) for the moment explosion time of SS, and T^α​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u) for the explosion time of the VIE (2.9).

Theorem 6.1.

Let u∈ℂu\in\mathbb{C}. Then Tα∗​(u)=Tα∗​(Re⁡(u))T^{*}_{\alpha}(u)=T^{*}_{\alpha}(\mathrm{Re}(u)), and (2.1) holds for 0<t<Tα∗​(u)0<t<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u).

Lemma 6.2.

Let u∈ℂu\in\mathbb{C}. Then T^α​(u)≥Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)\geq T^{*}_{\alpha}(u).

Proof.

Suppose that T^α​(u)<Tα∗​(u)\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)<T^{*}_{\alpha}(u). The VIE (2.9) translates into a two-dimensional real VIE for (Re⁡(f),Im⁡(f))(\mathrm{Re}(f),\mathrm{Im}(f)). As T^α​(u)<∞\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u)<\infty, we get from Theorem 12.1.1 in [19] that (Re⁡(f),Im⁡(f))(\mathrm{Re}(f),\mathrm{Im}(f)) explodes as t↑T^α​(u)t\uparrow\hat{T}_{\alpha}(u). This contradicts the continuity of t↦𝔼⁡[eu​Xt]t\mapsto\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{t}}], where the latter is shown as in the proof of Theorem 5.7. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

The first statement is clear from |eu​Xt|=eRe⁡(u)​Xt|e^{uX_{t}}|=e^{\mathrm{Re}(u)X_{t}}. Now let t>0t>0 be arbitrary. As above, we write M~\tilde{M} for the mgf and MM for the right-hand side of (2.1). By Theorem 5.7, we have M​(v,t)=M~​(v,t)M(v,t)=\tilde{M}(v,t) for vv in the real interval

I:={v∈ℝ:Tα∗​(v)≥t}.I:=\{v\in\mathbb{R}:T^{*}_{\alpha}(v)\geq t\}.

The function M~​(⋅,t)\tilde{M}(\cdot,t) is analytic on the strip

(6.1) {v∈ℂ:Re⁡(v)∈I}={v∈ℂ:Tα∗​(v)≥t}.\{v\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}(v)\in I\}=\{v\in\mathbb{C}:T^{*}_{\alpha}(v)\geq t\}.

By the same argument as in Lemma 5.4, the function M⁡(⋅,t)M(\cdot,t) is analytic on the set {v∈ℂ:T^α​(v)≥t}\{v\in\mathbb{C}:\hat{T}_{\alpha}(v)\geq t\}, which contains the strip (6.1) by Lemma 6.2. Therefore, M⁡(⋅,t)M(\cdot,t) and M~​(⋅,t)\tilde{M}(\cdot,t) agree on (6.1) by analytic continuation. This implies the assertion. ∎

7. Computing the explosion time

Recall that, for fixed u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, the explosion time Tα∗​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u) of the rough Heston model is the blow-up time of f⁡(t)=f⁡(u,t)=c3​ψ​(u,t)f(t)=f(u,t)=c_{3}\psi(u,t), where ψ\psi solves the fractional Riccati initial value problem (2.4)–(2.5). We know from Theorem 2.4 that Tα∗​(u)<∞T^{*}_{\alpha}(u)<\infty exactly in the cases (A) and (B), defined in Section 2. We now develop a method (Algorithm 7.5) to compute Tα∗​(u)T^{*}_{\alpha}(u) for uu satisfying the conditions of case (A). In case (B), a lower bound can be computed, which is sometimes sharper than the explicit bound (4.1). The function ff satisfies the fractional Riccati equation

(7.1) Dα​f=d1+d2​f+f2,D^{\alpha}f=d_{1}+d_{2}f+f^{2},

where d1​(u):=c1​(u)​c3d_{1}(u):=c_{1}(u)c_{3} and d2​(u):=c2​(u)d_{2}(u):=c_{2}(u), with initial condition I1−α​f​(0)=0I^{1-\alpha}f(0)=0. (Recall that we often suppress the dependence on uu in the notation.) We try a fractional power series ansatz

(7.2) f⁡(t)=!∑n=1∞an​(u)​tα​nf(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}(u)t^{\alpha n}

with unknown coefficients an=an​(u)a_{n}=a_{n}(u).

Lemma 7.1.

(see e.g. [21]) Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). The fractional integral and derivative of power functions are given by

(7.3) Itα​tν\displaystyle I^{\alpha}_{t}t^{\nu} =tν+α​Γ⁡(ν+1)Γ⁡(ν+α+1)for ​ν>−1,\displaystyle=t^{\nu+\alpha}\frac{\Gamma(\nu+1)}{\Gamma(\nu+\alpha+1)}\qquad\text{for~}\nu>-1,
(7.4) Dtα​tν\displaystyle D^{\alpha}_{t}t^{\nu} =tν−α​Γ⁡(ν+1)Γ⁡(ν−α+1)for ​ν>−1+α.\displaystyle=t^{\nu-\alpha}\frac{\Gamma(\nu+1)}{\Gamma(\nu-\alpha+1)}\qquad\text{for~}\nu>-1+\alpha.

By (7.3), the fractional power series (7.2) (formally) satisfies the initial condition (2.5). Inserting (7.2) into (7.1) and using (7.4), we obtain

∑n=0∞an+1​vn+1​tα​n\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n+1}v_{n+1}t^{\alpha n} =d1+∑n=1∞d2​an​tα​n+∑n=2∞(∑k=1n−1ak​an−k)​tα​n\displaystyle=d_{1}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_{2}a_{n}t^{\alpha n}+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_{k}a_{n-k}\Big)t^{\alpha n}
(7.5) =d1+d2​a1​tα+∑n=2∞(d2​an+∑k=1n−1ak​an−k)​tα​n,\displaystyle=d_{1}+d_{2}a_{1}t^{\alpha}+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\Big(d_{2}a_{n}+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_{k}a_{n-k}\Big)t^{\alpha n},

where

vn:=Γ⁡(α​n+1)Γ⁡(α​n−α+1).v_{n}:=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha n+1)}{\Gamma(\alpha n-\alpha+1)}.

Note that vnv_{n} is an increasing sequence; this follows easily from the fact that log∘Γ\log\circ\,\Gamma is convex (see Example 11.14 in [32]). By Stirling’s formula, vn∼(α​n)αv_{n}\sim(\alpha n)^{\alpha} for n→∞n\to\infty. From (7.5), we obtain a convolution recurrence for an=an​(u)a_{n}=a_{n}(u):

(7.6) a1​(u)\displaystyle a_{1}(u) =d1​(u)/v1,\displaystyle=d_{1}(u)/v_{1},
(7.7) an+1​(u)\displaystyle a_{n+1}(u) =1vn+1​(d2​(u)​an​(u)+∑k=1n−1ak​(u)​an−k​(u)),n≥1.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{v_{n+1}}\Big(d_{2}(u)a_{n}(u)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_{k}(u)a_{n-k}(u)\Big),\quad n\geq 1.

The function ff can thus be expressed as f⁡(u,t)=F⁡(u,tα)f(u,t)=F(u,t^{\alpha}), where

F⁡(u,z):=∑n=1∞an​(u)​zn.F(u,z):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}(u)z^{n}.
Lemma 7.2.

From the estimates in Lemma 7.2, it is clear that termwise fractional derivation of the series (7.2) is allowed, and so the right-hand side of (7.2) really represents the solution ff of (7.1) with initial condition I1−α​f​(0)=0I^{1-\alpha}f(0)=0, as long as tt satisfies 0≤t<R​(u)1/α0\leq t<R(u)^{1/\alpha}. We proceed to show how the explosion time Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) can be computed from the coefficients an​(u)a_{n}(u). The essential fact is that there is no gap between R​(u)1/αR(u)^{1/\alpha} and Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u). For this, we require the following classical result from complex analysis ([29], p. 235).

Theorem 7.3 (Pringsheim’s theorem, 1894).

Suppose that the power series F⁡(z)=∑n=0∞an​znF(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n} has positive finite radius of convergence RR, and that all the coefficients are non-negative real numbers. Then FF has a singularity at RR.

Theorem 7.4.

Suppose that u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} satisfies case (A). Define the sequence an​(u)a_{n}(u) by the recurrence (7.7) with initial value (7.6). Then we have

(7.10) lim supn→∞an(u)−1/(αn)=Tα∗(u).\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{n}(u)^{-1/(\alpha n)}=T_{\alpha}^{*}(u).
Proof.

Recall that f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot), the solution of (7.1), also solves the Volterra integral equation (2.9). From the references on smoothness cited before (5.16), it follows that f⁡(u,⋅)f(u,\cdot) is analytic on the whole interval (0,Tα∗​(u))(0,T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)). As f⁡(u,t)f(u,t) blows up for t↑Tα∗​(u)t\uparrow T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) by Proposition 3.2, and t↦F⁡(u,tα)t\mapsto F(u,t^{\alpha}) is analytic on (0,R​(u)1/α)(0,R(u)^{1/\alpha}), we must have R​(u)1/α≤Tα∗​(u)R(u)^{1/\alpha}\leq T_{\alpha}^{*}(u).

Assume for contradiction that R​(u)1/α<Tα∗​(u)R(u)^{1/\alpha}<T_{\alpha}^{*}(u). Then ff is analytic at R​(u)1/αR(u)^{1/\alpha}. But since z↦z1/αz\mapsto z^{1/\alpha} is analytic at R⁡(u)>0R(u)>0, the composition F⁡(u,z)=f⁡(u,z1/α)F(u,z)=f(u,z^{1/\alpha}) would be analytic at z=R⁡(u)z=R(u) as well, which contradicts Theorem 7.3. Therefore,

R​(u)1/α=Tα∗​(u).R(u)^{1/\alpha}=T_{\alpha}^{*}(u).

It is well-known that the radius of convergence is given by the Cauchy-Hadamard formula [29, p. 111]

R​(u)−1=lim supn→∞an​(u)1/n,R(u)^{-1}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{n}(u)^{1/n},

which concludes the proof. ∎

Note that, in case (B), we can argue similarly as in the preceding proof. However, the coefficients ana_{n} are no longer positive, and so Pringsheim’s theorem is not applicable. Then, the inequality R​(u)1/α≤Tα∗​(u)R(u)^{1/\alpha}\leq T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) need not be an equality. Still, we can compute a lower bound for the explosion time:

(7.11) lim supn→∞|an(u)|−1/(αn)≤Tα∗(u).\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_{n}(u)|^{-1/(\alpha n)}\leq T_{\alpha}^{*}(u).

Now assume that we are in case (A) again. We now discuss how to speed up the convergence in (7.10). Roberts and Olmstead [31] studied the blow-up behavior of solutions of nonlinear Volterra integral equations with (asymptotically) fractional kernel. Their arguments hinge on the asymptotic behavior of the nonlinearity for large argument. In particular, in our situation, with G⁡(u,w)G(u,w) from (2.10) satisfying G⁡(u,w)∼w2G(u,w)\sim w^{2} for w→∞w\to\infty, formula (3.2) in [31] yields

(7.12) f⁡(t)∼(?)Γ⁡(2​α)Γ⁡(α)​(Tα∗​(u)−t)−α,t↑Tα∗​(u).f(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{\sim}}\frac{\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}(T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)-t)^{-\alpha},\quad t\uparrow T_{\alpha}^{*}(u).

We write ∼(?)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{\sim}} for two reasons: First, our integral equation (2.9) does not quite satisfy the technical assumptions in [31]. Second, not all steps in [31] are rigorous. We proceed, heuristically, to infer refined asymptotics of an​(u)a_{n}(u) from (7.12). Define

Φ⁡(z):=∑n=1∞an​(u)​R​(u)n​zn,\Phi(z):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}(u)R(u)^{n}z^{n},

a power series with radius of convergence 11, by the definition of R⁡(u)R(u) in Lemma 7.2. Its asymptotics for z↑1z\uparrow 1 can be derived from (7.12). Recall that the explosion time and the radius of convergence of FF are related by Tα∗​(u)=R​(u)1/αT_{\alpha}^{*}(u)=R(u)^{1/\alpha}.

Φ⁡(z)\displaystyle\Phi(z) =f⁡((R​z)1/α)\displaystyle=f\big((Rz)^{1/\alpha}\big)
∼(?)Γ⁡(2​α)Γ⁡(α)​(Tα∗−(R​z)1/α)−α\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{\sim}}\frac{\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}(T_{\alpha}^{*}-(Rz)^{1/\alpha})^{-\alpha}
=Γ⁡(2​α)Γ⁡(α)​R−1​(1−z1/α)−α\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}R^{-1}(1-z^{1/\alpha})^{-\alpha}
∼αα​Γ​(2​α)Γ⁡(α)​R−1​(1−z)−α,z↑1.\displaystyle\sim\frac{\alpha^{\alpha}\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}R^{-1}(1-z)^{-\alpha},\quad z\uparrow 1.

The method of singularity analysis (see Section VI in [12]) allows to transfer the asymptotics of Φ\Phi to asymptotics of its Taylor coefficients an​Rna_{n}R^{n}. Sweeping some analytic conditions under the rug, we arrive at

an​(u)​R​(u)n∼(?)αα​Γ​(2​α)Γ⁡(α)​R−1​nα−1Γ⁡(α),n→∞,a_{n}(u)R(u)^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{\sim}}\frac{\alpha^{\alpha}\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\,R^{-1}\frac{n^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)},\quad n\to\infty,

and thus

(7.13) an​(u)∼(?)R​(u)−n−1​nα−1​αα​Γ​(2​α)Γ​(α)2,n→∞.a_{n}(u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{\sim}}R(u)^{-n-1}n^{\alpha-1}\frac{\alpha^{\alpha}\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)^{2}},\quad n\to\infty.

Numerical tests confirm (7.13), and we have little doubt that it is true (in case (A)). Summing up, Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) can be computed by the following algorithm, which converges much faster than the simpler approximation lim supn→∞an−1/(αn)\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{n}^{-1/(\alpha n)}:

Algorithm 7.5.

Let uu be a real number satisfying case (A).

  • •

    Fix nmax∈ℕn_{\max}\in\mathbb{N} (e.g. nmax=100n_{\max}=100),

  • •

    compute a1​(u),…,anmax​(u)a_{1}(u),\dots,a_{n_{\max}}(u) by the recursion (7.7),

  • •

    compute the approximation

    (7.14) (an​(u)​n1−α​Γ​(α)2αα​Γ​(2​α))−1α⁡(n+1)|n=nmax≈Tα∗​(u)\bigg(a_{n}(u)n^{1-\alpha}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)^{2}}{\alpha^{\alpha}\Gamma(2\alpha)}\bigg)^{\frac{-1}{\alpha(n+1)}}\bigg|_{n=n_{\max}}\approx T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)

We stress that, while the arguments leading to (7.13) are heuristic, we have rigorously shown in Theorem 7.4 that Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) is the lim sup\limsup of the left-hand side of (7.14). The heuristic part is that the subexponential factor n1−α×𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡n^{1-\alpha}\times\mathit{const} improves the relative error of the approximation from O⁡(log⁡nn)O(\frac{\log n}{n}) to O⁡(1n2)O(\frac{1}{n^{2}}). Note that our approach to compute the blow-up time can of course be extended to more general fractional Riccati equations. Finally, as mentioned above (see (7.11)), we can compute a lower bound for Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) if it is finite, but uu is outside of case (A):

Algorithm 7.6.

Let uu be a real number satisfying case (B).

  • •

    Fix nmax∈ℕn_{\max}\in\mathbb{N} (e.g. nmax=200n_{\max}=200),

  • •

    compute a1​(u),…,anmax​(u)a_{1}(u),\dots,a_{n_{\max}}(u) by the recursion (7.7),

  • •

    compute the approximate lower bound

    |an(u)|−1/(αn)|n=nmax⪅Tα∗(u)|a_{n}(u)|^{-1/(\alpha n)}\big|_{n=n_{\max}}\,\lessapprox T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)

    of the explosion time.

Remark 7.7.

As for the applicability of Algorithm 7.5, suppose that ρ<0\rho<0 (with analogous comments applying to the less common case ρ>0\rho>0). From (2.7), we have e0​(u)∼12​ρ​ξ​u>0e_{0}(u)\sim\tfrac{1}{2}\rho\xi u>0 for u↓−∞u\downarrow-\infty, and so we are in case (A) for large enough |u||u|. More precisely, case (A) corresponds to the interval u∈(−∞,λ/(ξρ)]u\in(-\infty,\lambda/(\xi\rho)]. For uu from that interval, the explosion time can be computed by Algorithm 7.5. To the right of u=λ/(ξ​ρ)u=\lambda/(\xi\rho), there is a (possibly empty) interval corresponding to case (B), where Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) is still finite, but Algorithm 7.5 cannot be applied. Still, a lower bound can be computed by (7.11), and we have the bounds from Theorems 4.1 and 4.2, which can be easily evaluated numerically. Proceeding further to the right on the uu-axis, we encounter an interval containing [0,1][0,1], on which Tα∗​(u)=∞T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)=\infty (cases (C) and (D)). Afterwards, Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) becomes finite again, but these uu belong to case (B), leaving us with bounds for Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{*}(u) only.

To conclude this section, we note that ff can be approximated by replacing the coefficients in (7.2) by the right-hand side of (7.13). Let us write bn​(u)b_{n}(u) for the latter. Retaining the first NN exact coefficients, this leads to the approximation

f⁡(u,t)\displaystyle f(u,t) ≈∑n=1∞bn​(u)​tα​n+∑n=1N(an​(u)−bn​(u))​tα​n\displaystyle\approx\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_{n}(u)t^{\alpha n}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(a_{n}(u)-b_{n}(u)\big)t^{\alpha n}
(7.15) =αα​Γ​(2​α)Γ​(α)2​Tα∗​(u)α​Li1−α​((t/Tα∗​(u))α)+∑n=1N(an​(u)−bn​(u))​tα​n,\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{\alpha}\Gamma(2\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)^{2}T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)^{\alpha}}\mathrm{Li}_{1-\alpha}\big((t/T_{\alpha}^{*}(u))^{\alpha}\big)+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(a_{n}(u)-b_{n}(u)\big)t^{\alpha n},

where Liν​(z):=∑n=1∞zn/nν\mathrm{Li}_{\nu}(z):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^{n}/n^{\nu} denotes the polylogarithm. While this approximation seems to be very accurate even for small NN (see [17]), it is limited to real uu satisfying case (A), and thus not applicable to option pricing.

8. Finiteness of the critical moments

While we have analyzed the explosion time of the rough Heston model so far, in most applications of moment explosions (see the introduction), the critical moments

u+​(T)\displaystyle u^{+}(T) :=sup{u∈ℝ:𝔼⁡[eu​XT]<∞},\displaystyle:=\sup\{u\in\mathbb{R}\colon\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{T}}]<\infty\},
(8.1) u−​(T)\displaystyle u^{-}(T) :=inf{u∈ℝ:𝔼⁡[eu​XT]<∞},T>0,\displaystyle:=\inf\{u\in\mathbb{R}\colon\mathbb{E}[e^{uX_{T}}]<\infty\},\quad T>0,

are of interest. Using the upper bound for the moment explosion time Tα∗T_{\alpha}^{\ast} in Theorem 4.2, we will now show the finiteness of the critical moments for every maturity T>0T>0. Computing u+​(T)u^{+}(T) and u−​(T)u^{-}(T) is discussed in Section 9.

Theorem 8.1.

In the rough Heston model the critical moments u+​(T)u^{+}(T) and u−​(T)u^{-}(T) are finite for every T>0T>0.

Proof.

Only the finiteness of u+​(T)u^{+}(T) is proven, as the proof for u−​(T)u^{-}(T) is very similar. Denote the upper bound of Tα∗​(u)T_{\alpha}^{\ast}(u) in (4.3) by B⁡(u)B(u) for all u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} in the cases (A) and (B). where ρ¯2=1−ρ2\bar{\rho}^{2}=1-\rho^{2}. Thus, eventually e1​(u)<0e_{1}(u)<0 for sufficiently large uu. In the next step, we show that the upper bound B⁡(u)B(u) converges to 00 as u→∞u\to\infty. Indeed, in case (A) the integral in (4.3) satisfies

for some c>0c>0, using the monotonicity G⁡(u,w)≥G⁡(u,0)G(u,w)\geq G(u,0), the inequality G⁡(u,w)≥w2G(u,w)\geq w^{2} and G⁡(u,0)=c3​c1​(u)∼12​c3​u2G(u,0)=c_{3}c_{1}(u)\sim\tfrac{1}{2}c_{3}u^{2} as u→∞u\to\infty.

If we are eventually in case (B) as u→∞u\to\infty, then −e1​(u)>0-e_{1}(u)>0 and −e0​(u)>0-e_{0}(u)>0 holds for all sufficiently large uu. Note that in this case G⁡(u,⋅)G(u,\cdot) attains its global minimum at −e0​(u)-e_{0}(u) and the minimum value is −e1​(u)-e_{1}(u). Thus, the integral in (4.3) satisfies

From the preceding proof, it easily follows that u+​(T)u^{+}(T) and u−​(T)u^{-}(T) are of order T−αT^{-\alpha} as T↓0T\downarrow 0. This is consistent with the classical Heston model (α=1\alpha=1), where the decay order is T−1T^{-1}, by inverting (2.13).

9. Computing the critical moments

We first collect some simple facts that apparently have not been made explicit in the literature on moment explosions. Moment explosion time and critical moments are defined as in (2.11) resp. (8.1).

Lemma 9.1.

Let S=(St)t≥0=(eXt)t≥0S=(S_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(e^{X_{t}})_{t\geq 0} be a positive stochastic process. Its moment explosion time is denoted by T∗​(u)T^{*}(u), u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, and its critical moments by u−​(T)u^{-}(T) and u+​(T)u^{+}(T), T>0T>0.

  • (i)

    T∗​(u)T^{*}(u) increases for u≤0u\leq 0, and decreases for u≥0u\geq 0.

  • (ii)

    If SS is a martingale, then u+​(T)u^{+}(T) decreases, and u−​(T)u^{-}(T) increases.

  • (iii)

    Suppose that SS is a martingale. If T∗​(u)T^{*}(u) decreases strictly on the interval

    𝒟+:={u≥1:T∗​(u)<∞},\mathcal{D}^{+}:=\{u\geq 1:T^{*}(u)<\infty\},

    then T∗=(u+)−1T^{*}=(u^{+})^{-1} on 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}. Analogously, if T∗​(u)T^{*}(u) increases strictly on the interval

    𝒟−:={u≤0:T∗​(u)<∞},\mathcal{D}^{-}:=\{u\leq 0:T^{*}(u)<\infty\},

    then T∗=(u−)−1T^{*}=(u^{-})^{-1} on 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}.

Proof.

(i) As T∗​(u)=∞T^{*}(u)=\infty, we may assume that u>0u>0 (u<0u<0 is analogous). The assertion follows from Jensen’s inequality, since x↦xv/ux\mapsto x^{v/u} is convex for 0<u≤v0<u\leq v.

(ii) We just consider u+u^{+}. Since SS is a martingale, we have u+≥1u^{+}\geq 1. For any number u≥1u\geq 1 and 0<T≤T′0<T\leq T^{\prime}, we have

𝔼⁡[ST′u]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[ST′u|ℱT]]≥𝔼⁡[STu]\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{\prime}}^{u}]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{\prime}}^{u}|\mathcal{F}_{T}]\big]\geq\mathbb{E}[S_{T}^{u}]

by the conditional Jensen inequality. This shows the assertion.

(iii) We just prove the first statement. Note that (i) implies that 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} is an interval. Now suppose for contradiction that u∈𝒟+u\in\mathcal{D}^{+} satisfies

u<u+​(T∗​(u))=sup{v:𝔼⁡[ST∗​(u)v]<∞}.u<u^{+}(T^{*}(u))=\sup\{v:\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{*}(u)}^{v}]<\infty\}.

This means that there is v>uv>u satisfying 𝔼⁡[ST∗​(u)v]<∞\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{*}(u)}^{v}]<\infty. Hence, T∗​(v)=T∗​(u)T^{*}(v)=T^{*}(u), contradicting the strict decrease of T∗T^{*}. Finally, suppose for contradiction that u≥1u\geq 1 satisfies u>u+​(T∗​(u))u>u^{+}(T^{*}(u)). Then there is 1≤v<u1\leq v<u such that 𝔼⁡[ST∗​(u)v]=∞\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{*}(u)}^{v}]=\infty. For arbitrary t≥T∗​(u)t\geq T^{*}(u), we get

𝔼⁡[Stv]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Stv|ℱT∗​(u)]]≥𝔼⁡[ST∗​(u)v]=∞.\mathbb{E}[S_{t}^{v}]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[S_{t}^{v}|\mathcal{F}_{T^{*}(u)}]\big]\geq\mathbb{E}[S_{T^{*}(u)}^{v}]=\infty.

This implies T∗​(v)=T∗​(u)T^{*}(v)=T^{*}(u), again contradicting the strict decrease of T∗T^{*}. ∎

If the assumptions of part (iii) hold, then we can compute the critical moments from the explosion time, by numerically solving the equations T∗​(u+​(T))=TT^{*}(u^{+}(T))=T resp. T∗​(u−​(T))=TT^{*}(u^{-}(T))=T. Note, however, that strict monotonicity may fail for reasonable stochastic volatility models. In the 3/23/2-model [25], the explicit characteristic function shows that the critical moments do not depend on maturity (for positive maturity), and the explosion time assumes only the values zero and infinity.

In the classical Heston model, on the other hand, it easily follows from (2.13) that T1∗​(u)T_{1}^{*}(u) (recall that the index denotes α=1\alpha=1) is a strictly monotonic function of uu: On the set where it is finite, T1∗T_{1}^{*} strictly increases for negative uu, and strictly decreases for positive uu. By part (iii) of Lemma 9.1, this implies that we have

(9.1) T1∗​(u+​(T))=TandT1∗​(u−​(T))=T,T>0.T_{1}^{*}(u^{+}(T))=T\quad\text{and}\quad T_{1}^{*}(u^{-}(T))=T,\quad T>0.

Thus, although the critical moments do not admit an explicit expression, they can be computed using (2.13) and (9.1), by numerical root finding with an appropriate starting value.

While we have no doubt that strict monotonicity of the explosion time extends to the rough Heston model, this seems not easy to verify. If we accept it as given, then the lower critical moment can be computed for ρ<0\rho<0 from

Tα∗​(u−​(T))=T.T_{\alpha}^{*}(u^{-}(T))=T.

Again, we focus on the lower critical moment, because then we can apply Algorithm 7.5 to compute Tα∗T_{\alpha}^{*} for ρ<0\rho<0. Recall that this algorithm works only for u≤λ/(ρ​ξ)u\leq\lambda/(\rho\xi), which amounts to case (A). Thus, TT must not be too large in (9), namely such that u−​(T)u^{-}(T) satisfies case (A). (Usually, this requirement is not too prohibitive.)

To provide some indication for the strict monotonicity of Tα∗T_{\alpha}^{*}, recall that according to Lemma 5.3, f⁡(u,t)=c3​ψ​(u,t)f(u,t)=c_{3}\psi(u,t) (see Section 2) decreases strictly w.r.t. uu, if u<0u<0 satisfies case (A). It is then plausible (although not proven) that the strictly smaller function f⁡(u2,⋅)f(u_{2},\cdot) explodes at a larger time than f⁡(u1,⋅)f(u_{1},\cdot), where u1<u2<0u_{1}<u_{2}<0. As another indication, the bounds in Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 are strictly monotonous, as seen by differentiating them w.r.t. uu.

Even in case strict monotonicity should not hold, we certainly have

(9.2) u−​(T)\displaystyle u^{-}(T) =sup{u<0:Tα∗​(u)=T}\displaystyle=\sup\{u<0:T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)=T\}
(9.3) u+​(T)\displaystyle u^{+}(T) =inf{u>1:Tα∗​(u)=T}\displaystyle=\inf\{u>1:T_{\alpha}^{*}(u)=T\}

for all T>0T>0, which suffices for numerical computations (under the above restriction on TT). The validity of (9.2) and (9.3) is clear from (5.16): If Tα∗​(⋅)T^{*}_{\alpha}(\cdot) is constant on some interval, lying to the left of zero, say, then the mgf blows up as uu approaches the interval’s right endpoint from the right.

10. Application to asymptotics

In the introduction we mentioned several potential applications of our work. In this section, we give some details on one of them: Knowing the critical moments gives first order asymptotics for the implied volatility for large and small strikes. We write σ^​(k)\hat{\sigma}(k) for the implied volatility, where k=log⁡(K/S0)k=\log(K/S_{0}) is the log-moneyness. According to Lee’s moment formula [23], the left wing of implied volatility satisfies

(10.1) T⋅lim supk→−∞σ^​(k)2|k|=2−4​(u−​(T)2−u−​(T)+u−​(T)).T\cdot\limsup_{k\to-\infty}\frac{\hat{\sigma}(k)^{2}}{|k|}=2-4\big(\sqrt{u^{-}(T)^{2}-u^{-}(T)}+u^{-}(T)\big).

We focus on negative log-moneyness, because then the slope depends on the lower critical moment, which Algorithm 7.5 computes in the important case ρ<0\rho<0. As in any model with finite critical moments, the marginal densities of the rough Heston model have power-law tails. More precisely, if we write fTf_{T} for the density of STS_{T}, then

fT​(x)=x−u+​(T)−1+o⁡(1),x→∞,f_{T}(x)=x^{-u^{+}(T)-1+o(1)},\quad x\to\infty,

and

(10.2) fT​(x)=x−u−​(T)−1+o⁡(1),x↓0.f_{T}(x)=x^{-u^{-}(T)-1+o(1)},\quad x\downarrow 0.

Our approach (see Section 9) allows to evaluate the right-hand sides of (10.1) and (10.2) numerically for the rough Heston model, if TT is not too large.

In [13], (10.1)–(10.2) were considerably sharpened for the classical Heston model. We expect that such a refined smile expansion can be done for rough Heston, too, with density asymptotics of the form

fT​(x)∼c1​x−u+​(T)−1​ec2​(log⁡x)1−1/(2​α)​(log⁡x)c3,x→∞,f_{T}(x)\sim c_{1}x^{-u^{+}(T)-1}e^{c_{2}(\log x)^{1-1/(2\alpha)}}(\log x)^{c_{3}},\quad x\to\infty,

where the cic_{i} depend on TT and α\alpha. In the classical Heston model, the factor ec2​(log⁡x)1−1/(2​α)e^{c_{2}(\log x)^{1-1/(2\alpha)}} becomes ec2​log⁡x,e^{c_{2}\sqrt{\log x}}, in line with [13]. Extending the analysis of [13] to 12<α<1\tfrac{1}{2}<\alpha<1 will require a detailed study of the blow-up behavior of the Volterra integral equation (2.9). Among other things, (a special case of) the heuristic analysis in [31], which we already mentioned in Section 7, would have to be made rigorous, and extended to ensure uniformity w.r.t. the parameter uu. We postpone this to future work. Note that the approximation (7.15) might be useful in this context.
